text: XGBoost isn't the only serious boosting library. LightGBM, from Microsoft, and CatBoost, from Yandex, are used just as widely, and each has a design choice that makes it shine in certain situations. All three implement the same core idea you already know -- what's different is how they grow trees and handle categories.

LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise instead of level-wise: it always splits the single leaf that reduces loss the most, reaching lower loss with the same number of leaves, but the trees become lopsided. That makes num_leaves its key complexity knob -- max_depth is a weaker control here than in XGBoost. Keep num_leaves small on small data.

Training LightGBM looks similar, with two differences: early stopping is a callback, lgb.early_stopping of thirty, and a pandas category column like plan is used natively with no encoding step. On our split it stopped at round one fifteen with a test A.U.C. of zero point eight three zero.

CatBoost's headline feature is native categorical handling: instead of one-hot encoding, it converts categories to numbers using target statistics computed with an ordered scheme that avoids label leakage. That matters most for high-cardinality columns like product I.D. or city. You tell it which columns are categorical with cat_features.

CatBoost stopped at round one twenty-three with a test A.U.C. of zero point eight three one. Comparing all three on one split: XGBoost zero point eight two eight, LightGBM zero point eight three zero, CatBoost zero point eight three one -- practically tied. Across five different splits, the averages were zero point eight three six, zero point eight three five and zero point eight three five, with about zero point zero zero six standard deviation.

The differences between libraries are far smaller than split-to-split noise, so on this small, mostly numeric table, don't pick by accuracy alone. Try LightGBM first on large datasets where training speed matters. Try CatBoost first with many categorical columns or when you want strong defaults with minimal tuning. XGBoost remains the mature, widely supported all-rounder.

The three libraries share the same boosting core. LightGBM grows leaf-wise and is fast, CatBoost treats categories natively, and XGBoost is the reliable default. On our data, accuracy was a tie, so choose by data shape, speed, and convenience. Next, we look at how to tune these models systematically.
